title: Snap two aluminium framing struts into a square corner, holding one still while pushing the other onto its connector
instruction: Join the two aluminium struts into a corner: hold strut A (the one running away from you, with the connector on its near end) still with one hand, and with the other push strut B's hollow end straight along the jig onto the connector's peg until the catch snaps up into the hole in its wall, keeping the corner square. Then let go of strut A, lift strut B so the whole corner rises in one piece, set the frame down flat on the table clear of the jig, let go, and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Machine frames, robot cells and test rigs are built from aluminium extrusion joined with push-in corner connectors. The strut being joined has to be held still against the push that snaps the catch, and the joint is checked by lifting the frame by the other strut.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) Strut A: a 20 mm square aluminium extrusion 26 cm long, 150 g, lying on the table running away from the arms, from 20 to 46 cm forward, 7 cm left of the centre line. On its near end, a die-cast zinc corner connector whose 11 mm square peg, 4 cm long with a pointed tip, points to the right, with a red spring catch standing 3 mm out of the peg's top. (2) Strut B: a 20 mm square aluminium extrusion 24 cm long, 130 g, lying square to A on its right, in line with the peg, its hollow end (a 14 mm square socket 4.6 cm deep, with an 8 mm hole in its top wall 1.1 cm in from the end) facing the peg, 1.5 cm short of its tip. (3) A framing jig: two dark steel strips 3.4 cm long and 1.6 cm tall, fixed to the table either side of strut B's end, 1.5 mm clear of it each side. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end. Fully on: strut B's open end within 3 mm of strut A's side with the catch up in B's hole. Square: the two struts' axes 90 degrees apart, within 3 degrees. 1.0: fully on and square, the corner lifted at some point after it snapped on, by strut B alone (strut A's near end at least 2.5 cm off the table with each gripper's fingertip centre (TCP) at least 5 cm from strut A), the frame lying flat on the table again, each TCP at least 5 cm from both struts, and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: fully on and square; 0.25: strut B at least 1 cm onto the peg; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with both struts still.
reset_notes: Press the catch down through the hole and pull strut B off the peg; lay both struts back where they started.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the extrusions are plain square bars with no T-slots; the spring catch is a small block on a sprung prismatic joint in the peg (1.5 N per mm), which strut B's wall presses down as it slides on and which springs up into its hole. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
